text.en: Ötzi died in the Alps around 3300 BC, about when writing appeared in Sumerian Uruk. By the time the Great Pyramid was built, he had lain in the ice for some 700 years.
When the Great Pyramid of Giza was built, woolly mammoths still lived on Wrangel Island — the last of them died out only around 2000 BC.
The Peruvian city of Caral, with its stepped pyramids, flourished in the same age as Egypt's pyramids — more than 4,000 years before the Incas.
Sargon of Akkad boasted that ships from Meluhha moored at his capital. That was most likely the Mesopotamian name for the Indus Valley, home of Mohenjo-daro.
Göbekli Tepe was built around 9500 BC, 6,500 years before Stonehenge. More time separates them than separates Stonehenge from us.
The Shigir Idol from the Urals was carved about 11,500 years ago. When the Great Pyramid was built, it was already almost 7,000 years old, older than the pyramid is today.
The mammoths painted in Chauvet Cave 36,000 years ago could still be seen alive in the age of the pharaohs: the last ones, on Wrangel Island, died out around 2000 BC.
Chinchorro fishermen on the Chilean coast were mummifying their dead by about 5000 BC; their mummies predate Egypt's by some two thousand years.

The oldest known customer complaint, from around 1750 BC, is about bad copper. A man named Nanni scolded the Ur merchant Ea-nasir for shoddy ingots and rude service; Guinness lists the tablet as the oldest complaint on record.
Possibly the first personal name ever written belongs not to a king but to an accountant. Tablets from Uruk around 3200 BC read: '28,086 measures barley, 37 months, Kushim'.
The oldest substantially complete piece of written music is about 3,400 years old: a hymn to the goddess Nikkal, notated in cuneiform on a clay tablet from Ugarit in Syria around 1400 BC.
The earliest named author in history was a woman: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god at Ur in the 23rd century BC, to whom hymns to Inanna are attributed.

The world's oldest leather shoe is 5,500 years old — and roughly a European size 37. Found in Armenia's Areni-1 cave, it was cut from a single piece of hide, still had its laces and was stuffed with grass.
The oldest known winery is some 1,500 years older than the Great Pyramid. It was found in Armenia's Areni-1 cave, home of the oldest shoe, where wine was made around 4100–4000 BC.
Some flutes about 9,000 years old can still be played. They were carved from the wing bones of cranes at the Neolithic village of Jiahu in China, where 33 of them have been found.
One of the world's oldest known alcoholic drinks was a cocktail of rice, honey and hawthorn. Residues on 9,000-year-old pottery from Jiahu, China, point to a cross between beer, wine and mead.
The oldest known noodles are about 4,000 years old. The thin yellow strands were found in 2005 in an upturned pot at Lajia on the Yellow River, a village buried by mudflows.
People were having their teeth drilled up to 9,000 years ago. A Neolithic graveyard at Mehrgarh in Pakistan held eleven molars from nine adults with holes drilled while they were alive.

The first dentist known by name served the king who built the first pyramid. Hesy-Ra, an official of Djoser, bore the title 'Great one of the dentists' — though it can also be read as 'Great one of the ivory cutters'.

Around 2250 BC a boy pharaoh wrote a letter bursting with impatience: he wanted a live pygmy. Young Pepi II promised the caravan leader Harkhuf a rich reward, and Harkhuf proudly carved the letter on his tomb.

Pepi II is often called the longest-reigning monarch ever: 94 years, from the age of six. But the figure comes from Manetho, writing some 2,000 years later, and firm records reach only about his 62nd year.
The first king in the Sumerian King List ruled for 28,800 years. The eight kings before the Flood reigned 241,200 years in total; only afterwards did reigns 'shrink' to mere centuries.
The Sumerian King List includes a woman ruler — a tavern keeper. Kubaba supposedly ruled Kish for 100 years under the title lugal, 'king', which had no feminine form.
The oldest known joke is a fart joke. A Sumerian proverb from about 1900 BC calls it unheard of since time immemorial for a young wife never to have broken wind in her husband's lap.

The oldest inscribed papyrus is a logbook of stone deliveries for the Great Pyramid. Inspector Merer noted how his crew shipped limestone from Tura to Giza by boat; the papyri turned up on the Red Sea coast in 2013.

The Great Pyramid was not built by slaves. Archaeologists think tens of thousands of skilled workers built it for pay or in lieu of taxes; shift workers received ten loaves of bread and a jug of beer a day.

Ancient Egypt had its own Egyptologist. Prince Khaemwaset, a son of Ramesses II, restored pyramids and tombs already over a thousand years old, including Djoser's, and re-inscribed the names of their forgotten owners.

A near-contemporary of Tutankhamun in China was an army general. Fu Hao, wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, led military campaigns and served as high priestess; her intact tomb, found in 1976, earned her the name 'the Chinese Tutankhamun'.

Some 14,000 years ago, people were already nursing sick dogs. A puppy buried with two humans near Bonn had survived canine distemper, which researchers say it could only have done with constant human care.
A cat was buried beside a human on Cyprus 9,500 years ago, nearly 6,000 years before the famous cats of Egyptian paintings. Cyprus had no wild cats, so people must have brought it by boat.
Przewalski's horse, 'the last wild horse', may not be wild at all. Genetics links it to the horses of Kazakhstan's Botai culture, kept by people 5,500 years ago, so it is probably feral.
People in Kazakhstan were drinking mare's milk almost a thousand years before the Great Pyramid. Traces of it on Botai pottery from about 3500 BC are among the earliest evidence of domestic horses.

A girl from Siberia's Denisova Cave had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. She lived some 90,000 years ago, died at about 13, and is the only first-generation hybrid of two human species ever found.

As recently as 50,000 years ago, humans about 1.1 metres tall lived on the Indonesian island of Flores. Nicknamed 'hobbits', Homo floresiensis descended from settlers who arrived a million years earlier and probably shrank.

A boy buried 24,000 years ago near Irkutsk was a genetic relative of both Native Americans and Europeans. His people, the Ancient North Eurasians, were partial ancestors of Native Americans and of Bronze Age steppe herders.

Human footprints in New Mexico are dated to 21,000–23,000 years ago, millennia before people were thought to have reached the Americas. Mammoth and giant sloth tracks lie beside them, though the dating is still debated.
The oldest known boat is about 10,000 years old. The three-metre Pesse canoe from the Netherlands was hollowed out of a single pine trunk with stone or antler tools between 8040 and 7510 BC.
Pots appeared 8,000–9,000 years before farming. Sherds from Xianren Cave in China are 19,000–20,000 years old, the earliest pottery known, made by hunter-gatherers at the end of the Ice Age.

A wooden causeway in England has been dated to the very year: 3807 or 3806 BC. Tree rings show the Sweet Track across a marsh was laid 1,250 years before the Great Pyramid, and was used for only about ten years.

Ireland's Newgrange is about 500 years older than both Stonehenge in its present form and the Great Pyramid. Once a year, at the winter solstice sunrise, light pours through a 'roofbox' above the entrance into its inner chamber.
One of Stonehenge's stones seems to have come from Scotland, nearly 700 km away. A 2024 study matched the Altar Stone to rocks of north-east Scotland; it had long been thought to come from Wales.

Stonehenge's bluestones were hauled from Wales, 240 km away — and may even be recycled. In Wales researchers found a dismantled stone circle of exactly the same diameter as the first Stonehenge: 110 metres.

Early Bronze Age Britain's richest grave was found near Stonehenge during a housing development, and its owner came from the Alps. Isotopes in the Amesbury Archer's teeth show he grew up in central Europe.
We even know the season when the Egtved Girl was buried in Denmark: summer, 1370 BC. The tree rings of her oak coffin say so, and a yarrow flower had been laid on it.
The first known zoo appeared in Egypt before the pharaohs. Around 3500 BC Hierakonpolis kept hippos, elephants, baboons, crocodiles and a leopard, whose burials were found in 2009.
In the middle of the Sahara, rock paintings show people swimming. The art in the Cave of Swimmers may be up to 10,000 years old, from when the desert was a green land of lakes, giraffes and hippos.

The first recorded strike took place in Egypt around 1170 BC. Royal tomb builders downed tools over late wheat rations — 'We are hungry!' The authorities heard them out, and work resumed the next day.
Rubber balls are at least 3,600 years old. The oldest were found in Mexico in the bog of El Manatí, where around 1600 BC the Olmecs cast offerings to the gods along with wooden busts and stone axes.

Football has a 3,400-year-old ancestor, as even FIFA's president has acknowledged. The oldest Mesoamerican ballcourt, at Paso de la Amada in Mexico, dates to about 1400 BC; its solid rubber balls weighed up to 4 kg.
Cacao was first used not in Mexico but in Ecuador, 5,300 years ago. The South American Mayo-Chinchipe culture domesticated it, and only later did it reach Mesoamerica, the Olmecs and the Maya.
Popcorn is about 6,700 years old. The earliest popping-corn cobs, from around 4700 BC, were found on the northern coast of Peru, two thousand years before Egypt's first pyramid.
Beer may be older than farming. Some 13,000 years ago the Natufians of Raqefet Cave near Haifa brewed a porridge-like beer for ritual feasts, before the first fields were sown.
Bread was being baked thousands of years before farming began. The oldest evidence of bread-making, about 14,500 years old, comes from a Natufian site in the desert of north-eastern Jordan.
The oldest beer recipe was written as a hymn to a goddess. A Sumerian song honouring Ninkasi, patron of brewing, is about 3,900 years old and describes making beer from barley bread.

A Babylonian student worked out the square root of two to six decimal places. The school tablet YBC 7289, from 1800–1600 BC, shows a square with its diagonals and the value 1.414213, off by less than one part in two million.

There are 60 minutes in an hour because of the Sumerians. Their base-60 counting arose in the 3rd millennium BC, passed to the Babylonians and survives today in minutes, seconds, degrees and coordinates.
Hammurabi's code was not the first. The laws of Ur-Nammu of Ur are some 300 years older, and instead of 'an eye for an eye' they set money fines for bodily injury.
One of the world's oldest towers is 10,000 years old. The 8.5-metre stone tower of Jericho was built around 8000 BC, some 5,400 years before the Great Pyramid.
Malta's Ġgantija temples are older than Egypt's pyramids, and locals said a giantess built them. In Gozo legend she ate nothing but broad beans and honey. The older temple is some 5,600 years old.

Ötzi, who died in the Alps 5,300 years ago, has 61 tattoos. They were punctured into the skin with soot, and many sit over worn joints and his lower back, so they may have been a pain treatment akin to acupuncture.
Ötzi's last meal is known down to its ingredients. Less than two hours before he died he ate ibex meat, confirmed by DNA, and his food also included einkorn wheat.

A puppy 18,000 years old turned up in the Yakutian permafrost with its fur and whiskers. Scientists could not tell if it was a dog or a wolf and named it Dogor, Yakut for 'friend'. In 2022 genetics said: wolf.
East Asia's oldest observatory is about 4,000 years old. At Taosi in China, slots in an ancient structure seem to have framed the sunrise on the solstices, helping keep a solar calendar.

At Dholavira in India archaeologists found a three-metre 'signboard' of ten Indus signs — and no one can read it. The Indus script is still undeciphered: not a single bilingual inscription has been found.

One of Egypt's first smooth-sided pyramids came out 'bent'. At a height of 47 metres, Sneferu's builders changed the slope from 54° to 43°, probably fearing collapse, creating the Bent Pyramid of Dahshur.

The female pharaoh Hatshepsut was portrayed as a man, with a male body and male dress. After her death her statues were smashed and her deeds credited to other kings in an attempt to erase her from history.

The oldest surviving cheese was found on mummies in the Taklamakan Desert and is about 3,600 years old. Cheese-making is older still: clay strainers with milk-fat residues from Poland date to about 5500 BC.

Stonehenge is older than the Great Pyramid. Its first circle, a ditch and bank, was dug around 3000 BC, over 400 years before the pyramid; the great stones went up at about the time it was being built.

The world's oldest gold treasure is nearly 2,000 years older than the Great Pyramid. The Varna jewellery from Bulgaria dates to about 4500 BC — as ancient to the pyramid builders as the time of Christ is to us.
Australia's Aboriginal eel traps are older than Stonehenge and the pyramids. The Budj Bim channels are at least 6,600 years old — roughly 1,600 years older than the first Stonehenge.

Britain became an island after Çatalhöyük was built. The sea swallowed the last of Doggerland, the land linking England to the continent, around 6200 BC — by then people had lived at Çatalhöyük in Anatolia for some 1,200 years.

While the Sumerians were inventing writing, people in China were building dams. Around 5,000 years ago the city of Liangzhu in the Yangtze delta raised a system of flood-control dams, among the oldest in the world.

The war chariot was probably invented not in Egypt or Mesopotamia but in the southern Urals. The oldest spoke-wheeled chariots, from Sintashta graves of about 2100 BC, are as old as the Great Ziggurat of Ur.

Around 2200 BC a single drought may have hit three civilisations at once. Many scholars link it to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, the end of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the decline of the Indus cities.
As Hammurabi was carving his laws, North Americans were piling up giant earthworks. The concentric ridges of Poverty Point in Louisiana were built around 1700 BC by hunter-gatherers who did not farm.
Dingoes reached Australia at about the time Queen Hatshepsut sent her ships to Punt. The oldest dingo remains are some 3,450 years old, and seafarers from Southeast Asia brought them.

As the Bronze Age crumbled around the Mediterranean, Mesoamerica's first civilisation was rising: Olmec San Lorenzo flourished from about 1200 BC, while Egypt barely held off the Sea Peoples around 1175 BC.
People sailed to Australia while Neanderthals still lived in Europe. Aboriginal ancestors arrived at least 50,000 years ago; the last Neanderthals vanished only about 40,000 years ago.
In Mohenjo-daro 4,500 years ago many houses had toilets linked to a citywide sewer system. London got a citywide sewer network only in the 1860s.
Soap is older than the Egyptian pyramids. Soap-like mixtures of fat and alkali were made in Babylonia around 2800 BC, while the first pyramid, Djoser’s, went up around 2670 BC.
